messages.subject: Lavaan newbie with SEM Errors!
messages.body_plain:
I am a newbie to R, SEM and lavaan and am as such struggling to understand the lavaan usage for an SEM model.

My initial queries:

1. Some of my variables are of orders of magnitude larger than some others. Lavaan quits with an error saying that the model does not converge. Do we always need to scale all values (log transform or such) so that they are comparable?
2. I tried scaling the variables (by log transform) and here is my model specification
modelsc <- '
# measurement model - latest =~ observed
trait  =~  slasc + twig.den
abioenv  =~  soil.n + soil.p + soil.k
bioenv =~ con10sc + het10sc
#regressions - y ~ x
gr.annual ~ bioenv + abioenv
trait ~ bioenv + abioenv
gr.annual ~ trait
#correlations - y~~ x
slasc ~~ leaf.n
'
#fit your sem
fitsc <- sem(modelsc, data = semdata, estimator = "MLR", std.lv <http://std.lv> = TRUE)

It converges, but still gives errors
ph and thus ignored: loopRotation; residuals; residScale; residEdge; CircleEdgeEnd
> fitsc1 <- sem(modelsc, data = semdata)
Warning messages:
1: In lav_data_full(data = data, group = group, group.label = group.label,  :
  lavaan WARNING: some observed variances are (at least) a factor 1000 times larger than others; use varTable(fit) to investigate
2: In lav_model_vcov(lavmodel = lavmodel, lavsamplestats = lavsamplestats,  :
  lavaan WARNING: could not compute standard errors!
  lavaan NOTE: this may be a symptom that the model is not identified.

3: In lav_object_post_check(lavobject) :
  lavaan WARNING: some estimated ov variances are negative

I then tried to get the summary and plot using the following command (from a tutorial video):

summary(fitsc, standardized = TRUE, rsq = 1)
semPaths(fitsc, "std", edge.label.cex=0.5, curveplot = TRUE, layout = "tree")

I get some results but I must say I am confused on how to interpret.

Also, I need to understand if my initial errors are a problem.

Can someone kindly help?
Thanks and Regards,
Sharada

messages.subject: Re: semTools update
messages.body_plain:
Dear all,
first of all, thanks for the amazing R packages 'lavaan' and 'semTools', Yves and Sunthud!
I want to apologise in advance that my question will be more a conceptual question rather than a 'lavaan' question!
I use 'semTools' and 'lavaan' (and the 'WLSMV' estimator and the option 'missing pairwise') for an EFA for ordered categorical data using the 'efaUnrotate' function and do the rotation using 'oblqRotate'. Am I correct that I can report the model fit from the unrotated solution (and the model parameter estimates from the rotated solution), because the model fit won't change by doing any rotation?
Thanks a lot!

Am Samstag, 4. Mai 2013 22:14:16 UTC+1 schrieb Sunthud Pornprasertmanit:
> Dear all,
>
> We have updated the semTools package to version 0.4-0. Here is the description of the update:
>
>
> This version is available in CRAN and KRAN. This version adds the methods to implement exploratory factor analysis (EFA) by the lavaan package. The efaUnrotate function is used to fit an unrotated EFA model. Then, the orthRotate, oblqRotate, or funRotate functions can be used to rotate the standardized loadings from the unrotated solution. Fitting EFA model by the lavaan package allows users to use functionality of the lavaan package, such as scaled chi-square values, diagonal weighted least square for categorical indicators, or full information maximum likelihood. The imposeStart function is added to use parameter estimates of an analysis result as starting values of additional analysis. For example, the parameter estimates from a CFA model can be used as starting values for a multitrait-multimethod model. The compareFit function is also added to build a template for comparing multiple nested and nonnested models in a nice table format. The table can be exported to a file (via the saveFile function) or a clipboard (via the clipboard function). The bug of the parcelAllocation and moreFitIndices functions are also fixed.
>
> semTools link:
> https://github.com/simsem/semTools/wiki
>
> Best,
> Sunthud

messages.subject: bi-factor cfa and multiple method factors
messages.subject_clean: bi-factor cfa and multiple method factors
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

I'm new to conducting CFA, and would be appreciative of any feedback users on this site could provide.  I've seen a few questions on here in the past that are similar but not quite the same to what I'll pose.  I'm trying to implement an approach used in a paper by Biderman, Nguyen, Cunningham & Ghorbani (2011) where they examined the structure of the big five personality traits.  In sum, they created a CFA model with 3 method bias factors (1 for all items, 1 for positive items, and 1 for negative items) in addition to the 5 personality factors.  I'd like to attempt something similar with my data.  Below is what I have so far where g is the general factor, method is the negative bias factor, method_p is the positive bias factor, and f1, f2, f3 are the three group factors.

Overall, I have a few questions.  (1) Broadly, does what I've done below seems reasonable? (2) I've fixed the variances to 1 and made the factors orthogonal.  Is doing so any different than adding orthogonal = "FALSE" to the CFA function? Finally, I'm using MLS as an estimator per Rhemtualla, Brosseau-Liard & Savalei (2012) as the scale items contain five categories; however, I've seen a lot of recent papers using DWLS when any sort of ordinal indicators are used...has any sort of consensus been reached with respect to what estimator should be used for ordinal data?

m1<- ' g =~Item3+ Item1+Item6+Item9+Item11+Item12+Item14+Item2+Item4+Item5+Item7+Item8+Item10+Item13+Item15+Item16+Item17+Item18+Item19+Item20

              f1  =~ Item1 + Item4 + Item5 + Item9 + Item14 + Item18 + Item19

              f2 =~ Item2 + Item8 + Item10 + Item13 + Item15 + Item17 + Item20

              f3   =~ Item3 +Item6+ Item7 + Item11+ Item12 + Item16

              method =~ Item2+Item4+Item5+Item7+Item8+Item10+Item13+Item15+Item16+Item17+Item18+Item19+Item20

              method_p =~ Item3+ Item1+Item6+Item9+Item11+Item12+Item14

              f1 ~~ 0*f2

              f1 ~~ 0*f3

              f1 ~~ 0*g

              f1 ~~ 0*method

              f1 ~~ 0*method_p

              f2 ~~ 0*f3

              f2 ~~ 0*method

              f2 ~~ 0*method_p

              f2 ~~ 0*g

              f3 ~~ 0*method_p

              f3 ~~ 0*method

              f3 ~~ 0*g

              method ~~ 0*g

              method ~~ 0*method_p

              method_p ~~ 0*g

              f1 ~~ 1*f1

              f2 ~~ 1*f2

              method ~~ 1*method

              method_p ~~ 1*method_p

              g ~~ 1*g

              f3 ~~ 1*f3'

fit1<- cfa(m1, data=cfa_complete[,2:21],std.lv <http://std.lv>=TRUE, estimator = "MLS")

I do not know what your data are or what you are trying to do, but to me your model does not make much sense.

Here you are defining the same latent variable twice using just a different name for it.

> > > NoAdvBran =~ Nutrients
> > > Area =~ Nutrients

Is this really what you want to do?

> > > Nutrients =~ Nitrate + Phosphate + Chl

I do not know what Chl means, but it nitrate and phosphate are probably distinct types of nutrients instead of unidimensional measures of one underlying latent variable, which the model states.

You would need to provide a lot more detail on what you are trying to do to get more help.

Mikko

If I have an observed variable y1 that is dependent on a factor, as in:
f1 =~ y1 (+y2 + y3 etc)
and I then refer to the same observed variable, as in:
y1 ~~ 0*y1
I know I am setting the residual variance of the variable y1 to 0, not setting the variable's total variance to 0.
If I use that observed variable as a predictor elsewhere in the model, as in:
f1 =~ y1
f2 ~ y1
am I using the whole of y1 to predict f2, or am I using the residual of y1 to predict f2?

messages.subject: Re: observed indicators as predictors
messages.body_plain:
Ed,
Interesting question.  I ran the following script to test my understanding.

require(lavaan)

simModel <- '
 f1 =~ 1*y1 + 1*y2 + 1*y3 + 1*y4
 x ~ .5*y1
 y1~~0*y1
 y2~~1*y2
 y3~~1*y3
 y4~~1*y4
 x~~1*x
 f1~~1*f1
'

simData <- simulateData(simModel)

fitModel <- '
 f1 =~ y1 + y2 + y3 + y4
 x ~ y1
 y2~~y2
 y3~~y3
 y4~~y4
 x~~x
 f1~~1*f1'

simFit <- lavaan(fitModel, data=simData)
summary(simFit)
lavInspect(simFit, what='free')

My understanding is that you are predicting x from y1, not the unique variance of y1.  The results seem to confirm this understanding as I am able to recover my effect coefficient.

Regressions:
                   Estimate  Std.Err  z-value  P(>|z|)
  x ~
    y1                0.496    0.044   11.382    0.000

If x were predicted from the unique variance, which is a constant, this would not occur.

I find the matrix representation helpful for thinking through these kinds of issues.

$beta
   f1 y1 x
f1  0  0 0
y1  1  0 0
x   0  5 0

I did not anticipate this but lavaan moved the effect of f1 on y1 out of the lambda matrix and into the beta matrix.  The corresponding element in lambda is zero.

I am assuming from the fact that you set it to zero that you did not want to model the effect of the unique variance on x (your f2).  If you wanted to model the effect of a non-zero unique variance, I think that you would need to set the unique variance to zero and then replace it with a latent variable serving the same purpose as the unique variance.

Are you getting anomalous results that suggest otherwise?

Keith
------------------------
Keith A. Markus
John Jay College of Criminal Justice, CUNY
http://jjcweb.jjay.cuny.edu/kmarkus
Frontiers of Test Validity Theory: Measurement, Causation and Meaning.
http://www.routledge.com/books/details/9781841692203/

messages.subject: RE: observed indicators as predictors
messages.body_plain:
Keith—

     No, it must be this way. I ran into a model that did this, and I got into a frantic state.

     But your simulation put me back on the right path. It is the whole observed variable, not its residual, predicting the dependent—I get the same parameter estimates whether I do the prediction in the presence of the factor or I us lm() and run the regression among the observed variables. Should have figured that out myself, but thanks for helping me stabilize.

--Ed Rigdon

From: kmarkus via lavaan [mailto:lavaan@googlegroups.com]
Sent: Friday, May 5, 2017 10:38 AM
To: lavaan <lav...@googlegroups.com>
Subject: Re: observed indicators as predictors

Ed,
Interesting question.  I ran the following script to test my understanding.

require(lavaan)

simModel <- '
 f1 =~ 1*y1 + 1*y2 + 1*y3 + 1*y4
 x ~ .5*y1
 y1~~0*y1
 y2~~1*y2
 y3~~1*y3
 y4~~1*y4
 x~~1*x
 f1~~1*f1
'

simData <- simulateData(simModel)

fitModel <- '
 f1 =~ y1 + y2 + y3 + y4
 x ~ y1
 y2~~y2
 y3~~y3
 y4~~y4
 x~~x
 f1~~1*f1'

simFit <- lavaan(fitModel, data=simData)
summary(simFit)
lavInspect(simFit, what='free')

My understanding is that you are predicting x from y1, not the unique variance of y1.  The results seem to confirm this understanding as I am able to recover my effect coefficient.

Regressions:
                   Estimate  Std.Err  z-value  P(>|z|)
  x ~
    y1                0.496    0.044   11.382    0.000

If x were predicted from the unique variance, which is a constant, this would not occur.

I find the matrix representation helpful for thinking through these kinds of issues.

$beta
   f1 y1 x
f1  0  0 0
y1  1  0 0
x   0  5 0

I did not anticipate this but lavaan moved the effect of f1 on y1 out of the lambda matrix and into the beta matrix.  The corresponding element in lambda is zero.

I am assuming from the fact that you set it to zero that you did not want to model the effect of the unique variance on x (your f2).  If you wanted to model the effect of a non-zero unique variance, I think that you would need to set the unique variance to zero and then replace it with a latent variable serving the same purpose as the unique variance.

Are you getting anomalous results that suggest otherwise?

Keith
------------------------
Keith A. Markus
John Jay College of Criminal Justice, CUNY
http://jjcweb.jjay.cuny.edu/kmarkus
Frontiers of Test Validity Theory: Measurement, Causation and Meaning.
http://www.routledge.com/books/details/9781841692203/

--

messages.subject: Re: WLSMV multiple groups 'measurementInvariance'
messages.body_plain:
> I needed to treat the variables (range 0-4) as continuous.

This paper suggests that may be viable, since you have 5 categories:

http://psych.colorado.edu/~willcutt/pdfs/Rhemtulla_2012.pdf

The paper does not investigate missing data though, nor multigroup models or invariance.

> One of the ML options didn't seem as an alternative to me, because I wanted to use missing="pairwise" and the variables are slightly skewed and kurtotic.

Using MLR corrects SEs and chi-squared for nonnormality, with near-nominal Type I error rates according to the paper above.  And using MLR allows you to set missing = "FIML"

> The next step was to use the function measurementInvariance to investigate the next steps, but it seems like there will be no option to use WLSMV, just DWLS if I am correct?

WLSMV is the DWLS estimator, along with robust standard errors and a mean (M) and variance (V) adjusted chi-squared.  But if you are treating your data as continuous, you can use robust ML (MLR).

I'm a bit of a newbie to lavaan, and have jumped into the deep end by trying to run a latent growth curve analysis on some panel data. I have been coming across a few problems, and wondered if anyone could help me diagnose them. The data is a binary outcome (economically active or not) at 3 time points. I'm also adding in other latent variables as time-independent predictors of intercept and slope, and some time-varying covariates too. My model code is:

M1 <- '
#Intercept and slope of time-varying DV
intercept =~ 1*Activity_t1 + 1*Activity_t2 + 1*Activity_t3
slope =~ 0*Activity_t1 + 1*Activity_t2 + 2*Activity_t3

#Other latent variables
lv1 =~ lv1_measure1
lv2 =~ lv2_measure1 + lv2_measure2 + lv2_measure3 + lv2_measure4 + lv2_measure5
lv3 =~ lv3_measure1
lv4 =~ lv4_measure1

#Regressions
intercept ~ lv1 + lv2 + lv3 + lv4
slope ~ lv1 + lv2 + lv3 + lv4

#Time-varying covariates
Activity_t1 ~ cv1_t1 + cv2_t1 + cv3_t1
Activity_t2 ~ cv1_t2 + cv2_t2 + cv3_t2 + cv4_t2
Activity_t3 ~ cv2_t3
'

Note that Activity_t1, Activity_t2, Activity_t3 are binary factors, but are set to ordered prior to the analyses. Also, lv3_measure1, lv4_measure1, cv3_t1, and cv3_t2 are categorical variables.

The issue is that, when running:
>fit_M1 <- growth(M1, df, group = "sex")

I get:
Warning messages:

  lavaan NOTE: this may be a symptom that the model is not identified.

  lavaan WARNING: some estimated ov variances are negative

4: In lav_object_post_check(object) :

The model itself runs, but obviously something is wrong, and the summary looks pretty bare. I presume there is a problem with the syntax itself, but there seems to be a lack of examples/tutorials using growth curve analysis for categorical data, other than the page on the lavaan website itself. If anyone has any suggestions of where to start debugging this, that'd be great.

Thanks in advance!

Matthew

messages.subject: Re: Differences Between SPSS and Lavaan Correlations.
messages.subject_clean: Differences Between SPSS and Lavaan Correlations.
messages.body_plain:
The issue isn't a lavaan (or SPSS) specific one. In your lavaan code both F and G are outcome variables. So the covariance between F and G in your model results is a residual covariance (and the correlations are residual correlations). There's no reason to expect that the residual covariance and the bivariate correlation are the same. If you look at the sample statistics lavaan is using in your models the correlation is the same:
cov2cor(inspect(fit, "sampstats")$cov)## gives the correlation between F and G of -.57

The other thing to note, is that your model has non-zero df, so the model implied covariance matrix and the data covariance matrix are different. In the model implied matrix, the correlation between F and G is different from the correlation in the data.
cov2cor(fitted(fit)$cov) ##the correlation in the model implied matrix is -.548

Alex

Model C syntax does not match the path diagram, for the same reason the lower Model B syntax does not.  The =~ operator specifies arrows pointing from the latent common factor to the indicators, whereas the <~ operator specifies arrows pointing from the "indicators" to the formative construct.  You would also have to fix the (residual) variances of x1-x5 in Model C for the model to be identified.  If you fix them to zero:

messages.subject: Re: lavPredict:Underlying statistics
messages.body_plain:
> I am unsure as to how LavPredict is using and arranging the model parameters in the regression model in combination with the new data to make these predictions?

These methods go back a while, so it is easy to Google the 3 methods ("factor score regression", "factor score Bartlett", "factor score empirical Bayes") described on the ?lavPredict help page.  You can also ask on SEMNET or search their archives for discussion.

http://www2.gsu.edu/~mkteer/semnet.html

> I am looking for a way that I can use a 3 of my indicator variables to predict the 4th in a way that takes into account the model implied relationships between the variables, which is why I am not just using multiple regression.

Your description is contradictory.  If you want to use 3 variables to predict the 4th, then you do want to use multiple regression.  In which case, just use the lm() function and use predict() on the output.  lavPredict() calculates factor scores, using all 4 indicators and all model parameters to generate them simultaneously.  I think it helps to understand that regression slopes and correlation coefficients between X and Y are all expressions of their covariances, scaled by a different number.  Here are the 3 ways to express their relationship in lavaan syntax and their corresponding formulas:

> X ~~ Y   = Cov(X, Y)
> X ~~ Y (standardized/correlation) = Cov(X, Y) / sqrt(Var(X) * Var(Y))
> X ~ Y    = Cov(X, Y) / Var(Y)
> Y ~ X    = Cov(X, Y) / Var(X)

Given the direction of the relationship is mathematically arbitrary (though the interpretation is substantively different), you can use Y to predict X even using the regression slope of a model where X predicts Y.  Factor loadings are regression slopes, and the "regression" method in lavPredict() is simply a multivariate extension of this idea.  However, there are numerous problems with factor scores because of factor indeterminacy (related to but distinct from rotational indeterminacy in EFA).  You can also find more information on SEMNET.

Terrence D. Jorgensen
Postdoctoral Researcher, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam
UvA web page: http://www.uva.nl/profile/t.d.jorgensen

First, test whether there is a problem.  Heywood cases can be caused by gross model misspecification or merely by sampling error when a residual variance is close to zero (or correlation close to +/-1) in the population.  If your model fits well AND the 95% CI for the negative residual variance includes positive values, then you can probably feel safe interpreting your other model parameters.

http://journals.sagepub.com/doi/abs/10.1177/0049124112442138

messages.subject: Re: Latent factor correlations
messages.body_plain:
> I was hoping to get the Factor1 phase1 correlation with Factor1 phase2 latent variable.

Are you modeling the different occasions as different groups?  The groups in a multigroup CFA are presumed independent of each other, so there are no cross-group correlations.  If you analyzed the same sample at phases 1 and 2, you need to model them in a single-group longitudinal CFA.  There is a longInvariance() function in semTools to help with that, although I don't think it will help you accomplish your goal (see below).

> I was hoping to use this information to evaluate test-retest reliability / construct stability. I'm guessing the best model to extract for this analysis would be model 3 (intercepts), even though the invariance model had mean level invariance.

Evaluating latent correlations only requires metric/weak invariance.

Terrence D. Jorgensen
Postdoctoral Researcher, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam
UvA web page: http://www.uva.nl/profile/t.d.jorgensen

messages.subject: Re: Fwd: Different standard errors between lavaan versions 0.5-20 and 0.5-21
messages.subject_clean: Different standard errors between lavaan versions 0.5-20 and 0.5-21
messages.body_plain:
On 05/12/2017 08:34 AM, Annika Wilhelmy wrote:
> Hi Yves,
>
> Thank you again for getting back to me regarding the problem that I
> posted on different standard errors when using different versions of
> lavaan. About a week ago, I sent you my R script and data. Have you had
> the chance to start investigate the differences?

Yes. It has to do with the status of the `exogenous' covariates in your
model. (As this is just a simple regression model, think: the predictors).

By default, lavaan treats exogenous covariates as 'fixed' (rather than
stochastic). This corresponds to fixed.x = TRUE. This has no impact on
the point estimates. In addition, this has no impact on the standard
errors, as long as we compute the classic (naive) standard errors. This
changes, however, if we use estimator = "mlm" to get robust standard errors.

When estimator = "mlm" is used, lavaan version 0.5-20 (and older)
implicitly changes the status of the exogenous covariates from 'fixed.x
= TRUE' to 'fixed.x = FALSE' when computing the standard errors (and
test statistic). Effectively, the possible non-normality of the
exogenous variables was then taken also into account.

(Note that in the technical literature on MLM, fixed.x = FALSE is always
assumed)

 From version 0.5-21 onwards, this was no longer the case. This was a
side-effect of the implementation of WLS with fixed.x = TRUE.

If fixed.x = TRUE (the default), the exogenous covariates are no longer
included in the computations to compute the robust standard errors. Only
the non-normality of the stochastic variables (here only 'fuattorg') is
taken into account. I believe this is the better approach. Usually (in
typical SEM models with lots of endogenous variables, and only a few
exogenous variables) this has little or no effect. In your case, it has
a fairly large effect presumably because the sample size is rather
small, and fuattorg is highly skewed.

To get back the 'old' (0.5-20) standard errors, simply add the fixed.x =
FALSE option. Of course, then you are treating the predictors as
stochastic, which may not be want you want.

To the best of my knowledge, lavaan 0.5-21 is doing the right thing (if
we use fixed.x = TRUE). But perhaps, the univariate case is somewhat
special, and I would need to study this further to be sure (and surely
before the release of 0.6, where the distinction between fixed.x = TRUE
and fixed.x = FALSE is even sharper). I am not even sure if estimator =
"mlm" makes much sense in the univariate regression case.

(As a sidenote: Mplus 3 and 4 give the same answer as lavaan 0.5-20,
while Mplus 5 and higher simply returns naive standard errors in the
univariate regression case, even if estimator = mlm is requested).

Some alternatives you may wish to consider:

- use se="bootstrap"
- consider a linearizing transformation of 'fuattorg'
- use ordered="fuattorg" (perhaps after some recoding) to see what
happens if you treat 'fuattorg' as an ordinal variable

Hope this helps,

Yves.

messages.subject: Re: Latent factor correlations
messages.body_plain:
Conal,
My suggestion would be that you do the following:
1. Pick one of the scales and run it using the longInvariance() function.
2. Re-run the same analysis using manual model specification.
3. Compare the results to confirm that you have correctly replicated the analysis.
4. Repeat 1 through 3 for the other scale.
5. Combine your manually specified models to incorporate both factors, allowing the factors to correlate.
6. Double-check any large differences from the single-scale results.
7. Report the two-scale result.

The longInvariance() help file lists the constraints added in each step.  The lavaan Tutorial Model Syntax 2 page explains how to impose constraints.

Keith

Keith A. Markus
John Jay College of Criminal Justice, CUNY
http://jjcweb.jjay.cuny.edu/kmarkus

Hi

You are making a multiple step process when you should do the SEM model in 1 model, without extracting factor scores.

First model: CFA, measuremnte model of your factors of interest, for example something like this. From this model you want to stablish that items are proper to define the latent constructs

mod1 <- '
engage1 =~ item1 + item2 +item3
engage2 =~ item4 + item5 +item6
fb1 =~ item7 + item8 +item9
fb2 =~ item10 + item11 +item12
'

Then, second model, your latent regression model, this model estimates the regressions between latent factors, as latent factors, instead of using factor scores

mod2 <- '
engage1 =~ item1 + item2 +item3
engage2 =~ item4 + item5 +item6
fb1 =~ item7 + item8 +item9
fb2 =~ item10 + item11 +item12

engage1 ~ fb1 + fb2

engage2 ~ fb1 + fb2

engage1 ~~ engage2

fb1 ~~ fb2
'

bye

messages.subject: semTools::reliability estimates greater than 1?
messages.body_plain:
Hello,

I'm helping a colleague of mine with a latent variable model and recommended computing omega coefficients for a scale.
The scale has two factors, one of which is the construct measured by the scale and the other is a reverse-wording method effect. Essentially:

rf =~ item1 + item2 + item3 + item 4r + item5r + item6r
negItems =~ item4r + item5r + item6r

When he runs semTools::reliability() on the cfa output from the above, it results in some weird omega coefficients:

              rf  negItems     total

omega  0.9744239 0.9049808 0.9593466
omega2 1.5488518 0.7885791 0.9593466
omega3 1.5433199 0.7885505 0.9559202
avevar        NA        NA 0.6950781

What's up with that?

messages.subject: Re: MeasurementInvariance in Blavaan
messages.body_plain:
> Is there a function in blavaan that corresponds to measurementInvariance in lavaan?

No, but if you can run the measurementInvariance() function (in the semTools package) first, then you can access the parameter tables to use in place of model syntax when running blavaan() or bcfa().

HW.model <- '
visual =~ x1 + x2 + x3
textual =~ x4 + x5 + x6
speed =~ x7 + x8 + x9 '

out <- measurementInvariance(HW.model, data = HolzingerSwineford1939,
                             group = "school", fit.measures = c("cfi","aic"))

bout.config <- bcfa(parTable(out[[1]]), data = HolzingerSwineford1939, group = "school")
bout.metric <- bcfa(parTable(out[[2]]), data = HolzingerSwineford1939, group = "school")
...

Terrence D. Jorgensen
Postdoctoral Researcher, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam
UvA web page: http://www.uva.nl/profile/t.d.jorgensen

messages.subject: Re: LAVAAN latent code please HELP!!!!
messages.body_plain:
> do you have any basic papers about negative variances (Heywood cases) and how fix them?

It is not the negative variance that should be fixed, but the model that produces it (if necessary).  If your model fits poorly, this may be the cause of the negative variance.  You can look at correlation residuals for clues about how your model fails:

resid(fit, type = "cor")

If your model fits well AND the confidence interval for the Heywood case includes acceptable (positive) values, then there is no evidence that anything besides sampling variability led to the Heywood case, in which case you should just leave it alone.  Forcing a negative variance to be nonnegative will bias other parameter estimates in your model, and it will also merely hide the problem if misfit is the cause.

http://dx.doi.org/10.1037/1082-989X.13.2.150

http://journals.sagepub.com/doi/abs/10.1177/0049124112442138

Terrence D. Jorgensen
Postdoctoral Researcher, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam
UvA web page: http://www.uva.nl/profile/t.d.jorgensen

messages.body_plain:
> What's up with that?

I don't know, but posting your model parameter estimates might provide clues.  Looking at the formulas in the documentation <https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/semTools/semTools.pdf>, it looks like omega 2 and 3 estimates could exceed 1 if you have negative variance estimates, or any omega estimates might be able to exceed 1 if there are negative residual covariances or if there are cross-loadings.  But I am not aware of a paper that explains this.  You could post on SEMNET to see if anyone has encountered omega > 1 before.

www2.gsu.edu/~mkteer/semnet.html <http://www2.gsu.edu/~mkteer/semnet.html>

messages.subject: Re: semTools::reliability estimates greater than 1?
messages.body_plain:
Thanks for your reply!

We observed no negative variance estimates, but there are cross-loadings.

We initially did the following (intuitively):
RF =~ rf_1 + rf_2 + ... rf_10r + rf_11r + rf_12r # All RF items
NegItems =~ rf_10r + rf_11r + rf_12r # Reversed items

Which resulted in that > 1 omega coefficient.

Doing it another way:
RF =~ rf_1 + rf_2 + ... rf_10r + rf_11r + rf_12r # All RF items
rf_10r ~~ rf_11r + rf_12r
rf11r ~~ rf_12r
Resulted in a nearly equal fit, but omegas < 1.
I'm not entirely sure why. So the method-factor approach produced weird omegas, but the residual covariance approach did not.

messages.subject: Re: semTools::reliability estimates greater than 1?
messages.body_plain:
A followup to this; I had my colleague re-run the method-factor approach, but force 0 correlation between NegItems and RF, and the reliability estimates are now sensible. It dawned on me that to ensure that the negItems factor is in fact just explaining variance due to reverse items and NOT variance due to RF, we had to force the two to be non-correlated. That intuition was seemingly correct.

I searched on semnet and didn't see any mention of omega estimates greater than 1, but some decent discussion about what reliability really even means in latent variable contexts, which was nevertheless interesting.

Thank you again; I think this issue is resolved.

messages.subject: Nested models and multiple modifiers
messages.body_plain:
Hi there,

I aim to test nested models.
Therefore, I try to fix the parameters I'm not yet interested in to 0 in the earlier models (using the 0* specification, direct effects in this case). These will be included in later models (not fixed to 0)

This is the code:

model1 <- '#direct effects
            Y ~ 0*X1 + cD*X1
                    + 0*X2 + cC*X2
                    + 0*X3 + cW*X3

            #mediator
            M ~aD*X1 + aC*X2 + aW*X3
            Y ~ b*M

            #indirect effect
            abD := aD*b
            abC := aC*b
            abW := aW*b

            #total effect
            totalD := cD + (aD*b)
            totalC := cC + (aC*b)
            totalW := cW + (aW*b)'

And the error:
Error in lav_partable_constraints_def(partable, con = LIST, debug = debug) :
  lavaan ERROR: non-free parameter(s) in variable definition(s): cD cC cW

The problem is solved when I remove the 'total effect' part, where these definitions (cD, cC and cW) are asked for.
However, can I still consider this a nested model if the total effects are removed all together? Or is there a better solution?

Thanks in advance!
Sven

messages.body_plain:
> Can someone make sense of that?

Have you tried simulating factor scores, then using those to generate latent response variables, then discretizing them with thresholds?  Then you could directly compare your actual factor scores to the estimates from lavPredict().  Due to factor indeterminacy, I would not expect factor score estimates to be very accurate with only a few indicators, regardless of sample size. messages.subject: Re: Nested models and multiple modifiers
messages.body_plain:
> However, can I still consider this a nested model if the total effects are removed all together?

Yes.  The user-defined parameters are not additional estimated parameters.  They are merely functions of estimated parameters.  Nesting only concerns actual estimated parameters.

> Or is there a better solution?

Well, you could remove the 0* parts and just leave the labels, then use the constraints argument to force those "estimates" to be zero:

model1 <- ' Y ~ cD*X1 + cC*X2 + cW*X3
... '

myConstraints <- '
cD == 0
cC == 0
cW == 0
'
fit <- sem(model1, data = myData, constraints = myConstraints, ...)

Not sure if that will work, but it might give you some extra flexibility to define a set of "myConstraints" for each model, although you could also just add the constraints to the model syntax itself.

Terrence D. Jorgensen
Postdoctoral Researcher, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam
UvA web page: http://www.uva.nl/profile/t.d.jorgensen

messages.subject_clean: General SEM and some syntax questions
messages.body_plain:
Anna,
I would strongly recommend investing some time in an introductory SEM textbook to put yourself of firmer footing.  Replicating analyses form the textbook can help build your comfort level with the software.  It is probably never a good idea to learn SEM by attempting to complete your own analysis.  It is better to practice on data for which you know the result.

(1) There are two things worth distinguishing here.  'Composite' is the preferred term for a latent variable that is simply a (possibly weighted) sum of observed variables with no residual variance.  If you want to model some residual variance in the latent variable then you have a formative measurement model.  It sounds as if either could be applied to your data.  Note that such models treat the observed variables as exogenous variables.  So, you are not modelling their relationships.

The tutorial appears a little out of date but the <~ syntax is documented in the model.syntax help file.  As stated there in point 7, it generates a composite variable with the residual variance fixed to zero.

(2) You may have the right idea in your head but you are not using the right language to express it.  The model you are testing differs from the baseline model.  The model you are testing may be referred to as the focal model or target model.  The baseline model is a separate model used for comparative fit indices and is generally more restrictive than your target model.  As a result, it is possible for your model to fit and the baseline model not to fit the same data.  However, you are correct that a p value below alpha for either model can be taken as indicating that the respective model does not fit the data.

(3) SEM is a confirmatory method (for the most part) rather than exploratory.  You cannot test your model on the same data used to generate the hypothesis.  However, modification indices and expected parameter change statistics can help suggest ideas.  These are based on the impact of freeing a single parameter and can suggest redundant alternatives.  So, it is best to change one at a time.  Also, it is generally best to use these in tandem with other diagnostics such as residuals and a careful analysis of the constraints implied by your model.

(4) The best way to answer these kinds of questions is to feed the examples to lavaan and compare the output

> # Lavaan Group Question

+ Apples <- '
+ comp_var <~ 1*x1+x2+x3
+ y~comp_var
+ y~x4'

+ lavInspect(Apples.nofit, 'free')

The beta matrices appear identical.  So, lavaan seems to interpret the two model syntax objects the same way.  However, I would consider it good form to write model syntax with only one equation for each endogenous variable.  You can list the same variable twice in the equation for a variable when necessary.  See "multiple modifiers" in the model.syntax help file.

(5) This is probably the most common warning in SEM.  Let's take a closer look at you model using the same method as above and also the lavaanify() function.

The first thing to notice is that the model does not include a residual variance for y, this is fixed to zero.  Once you free that, you will find that the model has -1 degrees of freedom.  You have 4 observed covariances (y with each x variable because y is the only modeled variable) but five effect parameters.  These are labeled as p1 though p5 in the above table and numbered 1 to 5 in the beta matrix.  (The observed variance of y is used to estimate the residual variance of y.)  You may need a second outcome variable in order to identify the parameters in your model.

It can be a little tricky thinking about df when fixed.x = TRUE because it does not match textbook presentations.  You could try respecifying the model for fixed.x=FALSE as an exercise to allow you to count df in the textbook fashion.

Hello,

I have a multiple mediation model with 2 mediators and one binary endogenous variable (Y). I wanted to calculate the two indirect paths, the direct one and the total. Since my Y is binary (0,1), I calculated probit... My question is: can I also use glm function with family=binomial and link=probit?
 http://www.da.ugent.be/cvs/pages/en/Presentations/Presentation%20Yves%20Rosseel.pdf

What is the best way to know the p and Chi2 of my indirect and direct paths?
I tried with probit 11, 10, 00 (not sure if those scripts make sense).

Thanks in advance.

I.

mmodel <- 'Coex~c*log_size +b*M1 + e*M2
M1~a*log_size
M2~d*log_size
indirect1 := a*b
indirect2 := d*e
total   := c + (a*b) + (d*e)

probit10 := (-b0+c )/sqrt(b^2+1)
probit00 := (-b0 )/sqrt(b^2+1)
indirect := pnorm(probit11) - pnorm(probit10)

Em terça-feira, 16 de maio de 2017 10:41:12 UTC+2, Terrence Jorgensen escreveu:
> > do you have any basic papers about negative variances (Heywood cases) and how fix them?
>
> It is not the negative variance that should be fixed, but the model that produces it (if necessary).  If your model fits poorly, this may be the cause of the negative variance.  You can look at correlation residuals for clues about how your model fails:
>
> resid(fit, type = "cor")
>
> If your model fits well AND the confidence interval for the Heywood case includes acceptable (positive) values, then there is no evidence that anything besides sampling variability led to the Heywood case, in which case you should just leave it alone.  Forcing a negative variance to be nonnegative will bias other parameter estimates in your model, and it will also merely hide the problem if misfit is the cause.
>
> http://dx.doi.org/10.1037/1082-989X.13.2.150
>
> http://journals.sagepub.com/doi/abs/10.1177/0049124112442138
>
> Terrence D. Jorgensen
> Postdoctoral Researcher, Methods and Statistics
> Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam

Hi all!

I recently started with R, whereas in the past i used SPSS and (to a certain extend) AMOS. However, now i am working with R and still in discovery mode.
Currently i am busy with some analyses but i can't figure out what to do next.
The following steps i have undertaken:
The measurement model has been specified, and i now want to measure the differences in mediation output between the two groups in my study.
But i don't know how to do it. I thought of making a subset dataset for each group, do a mediation sem but then the results will differ i think. So my syntax is as follow:

#Measuring general model
model <- 'purposivevalue =~ purpval_1 + purpval_2 + purpval_3
sensebelonging =~ SoB_1 + SoB_2 + SoB_3 + SoB_4 + SoB_5'

fit.general<-cfa(model, data = spss)
summary(fit.general, fit.measures = TRUE, standardized = TRUE, rsquare = TRUE)

#subsetting the model to measure model per group
independent =subset(spss, selfconstrual=="1")
interdependent =subset(spss, selfconstrual=="2")

#Measuring the model for independent self-construal
fit.independent<-cfa(model, data = independent)
summary(fit.independent, fit.measures = TRUE, standardized = TRUE, rsquare = TRUE)

#Measuring the model for interdependent self-construal
fit.interdependent<-cfa(model, data = interdependent)
summary(fit.interdependent, fit.measures = TRUE, standardized = TRUE, rsquare = TRUE)

#Measuring the model for configural equivalence
fit.config<-cfa(model, data = spss, group ="selfconstrual")
summary(fit.config, fit.measures = TRUE, standardized = TRUE, rsquare = T)

#Measuring the model for metric equivalence: set the factor loadings equal across groups
# Show selected fit measures
fit.metric<-cfa(model, data=spss, group="selfconstrual", group.equal=c("loadings"))
summary(fit.metric, fit.measures = TRUE, standardized = TRUE, rsquare = T)
anova (fit.config, fit.metric)
#extract the list of parameters with operators
fit.metric.parameters <-parameterestimates(fit.metric)
fit.metric.parameters
#extract modification indices
modificationindices(fit.metric, sort. = TRUE)
fit.metric.mi <-modindices (fit.metric)
fit.metric.mi

#Measuring the model for scalar equivalence
fit.scalar<-cfa(model, data=spss, meanstructures = TRUE, group="selfconstrual", group.equal=c("loadings", "intercepts"))
summary(fit.scalar, fit.measures = TRUE, standardized = TRUE, rsquare = T)
anova(fit.metric, fit.scalar)

#extracting modification indices

fit.scalar.mi
modificationindices(fit.scalar, sort. = TRUE)

#Measuring the model for strict equivalence
fit.strict<-cfa(model, data=spss, group="selfconstrual", group.equal=c("loadings", "intercepts", "residuals"))
summary(fit.strict, fit.measures = TRUE, standardized = TRUE, rsquare = T)
anova(fit.scalar, fit.strict)

#extracting modification indices
fit.strict.mi <-modindices (fit.strict)
fit.strict.mi
modificationindices(fit.strict, sort. = TRUE)

#Measuring the model for partial strict equivalence
fit.strict.partial<-cfa(model, data=spss, group="selfconstrual", group.equal=c("loadings","intercepts","residuals"), group.partial=c("SoB_1 ~~ SoB_4"))
summary(fit.strict.partial, fit.measures = TRUE, standardized = TRUE, rsquare = T)
anova(fit.strict, fit.strict.partial)

#Modification indices do not help a lot to improve the model, as does a strict model approach.
#Therefore we will continue with the scalar equivalance and we base our model opon that.

model.mediation2 <- 'purposivevalue =~ purpval_1 + purpval_2 + purpval_3
sensebelonging =~ SoB_1 + SoB_2 + SoB_3 + SoB_4 + SoB_5
sensebelonging ~ a*age
purposivevalue ~ b*sensebelonging + c*age

indirect := a*b
direct := c
total := c + (a*b)'

fitmediationgeneral2 <- sem(model.mediation2, data=spss)
summary(fitmediationgeneral2, rsq=T, standardized = T, fit.measures = TRUE)

fitmediationgroup2 <- sem(model.mediation2, data=spss, group="selfconstrual", group.equal=c("loadings", "intercepts"))
summary(fitmediationgroup2, rsq=T, standardized = T, fit.measures = TRUE)

messages.body_plain:
Jorge,

require(lavaan)

# The Holzinger and Swineford (1939) example
HS.model <- ' visual  =~ x1 + x2 + x3
              textual =~ x4 + x5 + x6
              speed   =~ x7 + x8 + x9 '

fit <- lavaan(HS.model, data=HolzingerSwineford1939,
              auto.var=TRUE, auto.fix.first=TRUE,
              auto.cov.lv.x=TRUE)

my.CR <- function(fit, ...){

  l<-inspect(fit,"coef")$lambda
  v<-diag(inspect(fit,"coef")$theta)

  ll <- colSums(l)^2
  vm <- v %*% t(rep(1,length(ll)))
  sl <- sign(l^2)
  vv <- colSums(sl * vm)
  rr <- ll / (ll + vv)
  return(rr)
}

my.CR(fit)

   visual   textual     speed
0.6734319 0.8872648 0.8516294

If I am not mistaken, however, the equation that you gave only applies when the model has simple structure (no cross-loadings).  You would need to modify the function to handle more complex cases.

Keith

messages.subject: Constrain standardized loadings?
messages.body_plain:
responding to a post on github:
> Hopefully a quick question:
> Is it possible to constrain standardized loadings to be equal to one another in a CFA model?
> My understanding is that this is not possible, but I wanted to double-check. Thanks in advance.
> Jonathan

Not directly.  "Standardized" is unfortunately associated with scaling variables relative to sample-specific summary statistics rather than constant quantities, bring their generalizability into question.  If you have no qualms about the validity of testing constraints on such standardized estimates, it is possible to impose constraints rather indirectly on standardized estimates by

labeling any relevant parameters
using the := operator to define any necessary values (e.g., the model-implied total variance), and subsequently
defining the standardized estimates as user-defined parameters, which can then be constrained to equality (across groups, I presume?)
If you understand how model-implied (co)variances are calculated from model parameters, and that covariances are standardized to a correlation metric by dividing by the product of respective SDs, and that direct paths/slopes are standardized by multiplying by the ratio of predictor SD to outcome SD, here is a simple syntax example of each (didactic only, using a model that would not actually converge):

factor =~ c(1, 1)*x1 + c(L2.g1, L2.g2)*x2
factor ~~ c(PS1.g1, PS1.g2)*factor
x1 ~~ c(TH12.g1, TH12.g2)*x2
x1 ~~ c(TH1.g1, TH1.g2)*x1
x2 ~~ c(TH2.g1, TH2.g2)*x2

## define parameters in group 1
x2.total.var.g1 := L2.g1 * PS1.g1 * L2.g1 + TH2.g1
std.L2.g1 := L2.g1 * (PS1.g1 / x2.total.var.g1)
std.TH12.g1 := TH12.g1 / sqrt(TH1.g1 * TH2.g1)
## repeat for group 2, using ".g2" suffix instead

## constrain to equality
std.L2.g1 == std.L2.g2
std.TH12.g1 == std.TH12.g2

Terrence D. Jorgensen
Postdoctoral Researcher, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam
UvA web page: http://www.uva.nl/profile/t.d.jorgensen

messages.subject: Re: Multigroup mediation SEM
messages.body_plain:
> 1. How do i measure the (significant) differences between group 1 and group 2 regarding mediation output? (i thought of something with the anova function, but not sure how).

I'm not sure I understand your question.  There is a significance test reported to the right of the estimates.  If you want to test whether the indirect path (or a and/or b paths) differ significantly between groups, then yes, you can fit another model where you assign different labels for each group (so they are not constrained to equality, like they are in your model), then use anova() to compare the fit of the models to test the null hypothesis that the more constrained model fits just as well as the less constrained model.

> 2. The 'defined' parameters output, does this regard the total model?

It regards the parameters you defined.  Because you assigned the same labels (a and b) for both groups, they are constrained to equality across groups.

http://lavaan.ugent.be/tutorial/groups.html

If you give those parameters different labels in each group, you will have to define the indirect and total effects separately for each group, and both will show up in the output.

Terrence D. Jorgensen
Postdoctoral Researcher, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam
UvA web page: http://www.uva.nl/profile/t.d.jorgensen

messages.subject_clean: "Thurstonian IRT-model for binary forced choice data" - computable in lavaan?
messages.body_plain:
> how can I label the scales y* in the "theta" parameterization and put constraints on them?

y1 ~*~ c(scale1, scale1)*y1

Keep in mind, though, that the first group's scales will always be fixed by default, and only other groups' scale parameters will be freed after applying equality constraints to measurement parameters.  Here is an example that frees the scale parameters for 1 item and constrains them to equality, rather than fixing the first to 1 and freeing the second (the default).

myData <- read.table("http://www.statmodel.com/usersguide/chap5/ex5.16.dat")
names(myData) <- c("u1","u2","u3","u4","u5","u6","x1","x2","x3","g")

model <- '
  f1 =~ u1 + u2 + u3
  f2 =~ u4 + u5 + u6
'
fit1 <- cfa(model, data = myData, ordered = paste0("u", 1:6),
            group = "g", group.equal = c("loadings","thresholds"))
summary(fit1, fit.measures = TRUE, standardized = TRUE)

scales <- ' u1 ~*~ c(NA, NA)*u1 + c(scale1, scale1)*u1 '
fit2 <- cfa(c(model, scales), data = myData, ordered = paste0("u", 1:6),
            group = "g", group.equal = c("loadings","thresholds"))
summary(fit2, fit.measures = TRUE, standardized = TRUE)

Note that these are not statistically equivalent -- the second fits way worse, with the same df = 18.  The first model shows the latent scales are quite different, so the worse fit makes sense, but I can't think of how to test the equivalence assumption.  But I'm not sure if that is what you are need to run a Thurstonian IRT model.

Terrence D. Jorgensen
Postdoctoral Researcher, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam
UvA web page: http://www.uva.nl/profile/t.d.jorgensen

Jorge,
I am not sure that I understand the question.  However, I notice that the equation you gave for CR is identical to equation 6.20b for omega given by McDonald 1999.  If both reliability estimates are conceptualized as factor-expained variance divided by total score variance then it is just a matter of two equations for the same quantity: one equation being a special case of a more general equation, based on simplifying assumptions. Many thanks for your reply. It is really informative and helped me understand various aspects.

Anna

On Sunday, May 21, 2017 at 5:05:24 PM UTC+3, kma...@aol.com wrote:
> Anna,
> I would strongly recommend investing some time in an introductory SEM textbook to put yourself of firmer footing.  Replicating analyses form the textbook can help build your comfort level with the software.  It is probably never a good idea to learn SEM by attempting to complete your own analysis.  It is better to practice on data for which you know the result.
>
> (1) There are two things worth distinguishing here.  'Composite' is the preferred term for a latent variable that is simply a (possibly weighted) sum of observed variables with no residual variance.  If you want to model some residual variance in the latent variable then you have a formative measurement model.  It sounds as if either could be applied to your data.  Note that such models treat the observed variables as exogenous variables.  So, you are not modelling their relationships.
>
> The tutorial appears a little out of date but the <~ syntax is documented in the model.syntax help file.  As stated there in point 7, it generates a composite variable with the residual variance fixed to zero.
>
> (2) You may have the right idea in your head but you are not using the right language to express it.  The model you are testing differs from the baseline model.  The model you are testing may be referred to as the focal model or target model.  The baseline model is a separate model used for comparative fit indices and is generally more restrictive than your target model.  As a result, it is possible for your model to fit and the baseline model not to fit the same data.  However, you are correct that a p value below alpha for either model can be taken as indicating that the respective model does not fit the data.
>
> (3) SEM is a confirmatory method (for the most part) rather than exploratory.  You cannot test your model on the same data used to generate the hypothesis.  However, modification indices and expected parameter change statistics can help suggest ideas.  These are based on the impact of freeing a single parameter and can suggest redundant alternatives.  So, it is best to change one at a time.  Also, it is generally best to use these in tandem with other diagnostics such as residuals and a careful analysis of the constraints implied by your model.

> (4) The best way to answer these kinds of questions is to feed the examples to lavaan and compare the output

> 10 10       x1 ~~       x2    0     1     1    0     NA   1        .p10.
> 11 11       x1 ~~       x3    0     1     1    0     NA   1        .p11.

messages.subject: Re: MLM and mean structure
messages.body_plain:
Perhaps related to this thread as I've been searching to see if anyone else has noticed this (example attached).

lavaan() with "MLM" will automatically add meanstructure, but will not free the observed variable intercept terms unless one does additional changes to the model or other options. cfa() apparently doesn't have this feature. I noticed this a while back and am just getting around to asking whether this qualifies as a bug (it may at least be unexpected behavior). If one fits a model with ML and then just changes ML to MLM, it can result in really bad fit and may take a while to figure out that intercepts were added, but fixed all to 0.

On Monday, May 2, 2016 at 2:59:17 PM UTC-4, Yves Rosseel wrote:
> On 05/02/2016 08:40 PM, Mariella Sciortino wrote:
> > Dear Yves,
> >
> > Could you kindly give me a reference to the theory behind why
> > MLM estimation requires mean structure please?
>
> For MLM, as far as I can tell, a meanstructure is not needed in theory.
> This is just an implementational issue: in lavaan, the (old) code for
> the Satorra-Bentler test statistic insists on having a meanstructure.
>
> The new code (which is not used yet in 0.5-20), does not need this
> anymore. You can try this out by fitting a model with no meanstructure,
> and estimator = "ML", and then type:
>
> lavaan:::lav_test_satorra_bentler(fit)$satorra.benter
>
> Once the 'old' functions get replaced by the 'new' functions, this
> limitation will go away.
>
> Then again, using a meanstructure never hurts.
>
> Yves.
>

messages.subject: Re: Composite reliability (CFA)
messages.body_plain:
I'm honestly a bit confused about McDonald's omega. I understand hierarchical omega, essentially the reliability of a general factor after accounting for various subfactors. I'm not certain how the formula in reliability() achieves that, but I can say that hierarchical omega is not conceptually the same as omega1 and omega2.
Omega1 and omega2 are more similar to each other than they are to hierarchical omega.

All reliability is "true variance" over "some metric of total variance".
Omega1 and omega2 differ in how they specify total variance.
Omega1: Total variance is the explained variance from the factor of interest plus residual error plus residual covariance.
Omega2: Total variance is obtained from the full implied covariance matrix.

These can have important differences. As mentioned in the docs, Omega1's reliability uses variance after controlling for other factors. Omega2's reliability uses total implied variance from all factors. Omega1, then, is conceptually similar to "reliability of a measure after accounting for another factor", and omega2 is "reliability of a measure without controlling for another factor". I think, anyway.

Of these, I think omega2 makes much more sense, and I tend to prefer it. Composite reliability should be a metric of "if I were to compute sumscores/meanscores, what percent of variance is due to the underlying factor", and to me omega2 is more useful for this usecase, because if you *were* to compute sum scores, I don't think you would compute them after controlling for other factors, which omega1 is implicitly assuming.

Hierarchical omega, as I understand it, is quite different from these. By using the observed covariance matrix, it's likely that hierarchical omega will be a conservative estimate anyway. And hierarchical omega, I think anyway, is meant to be used for cases where you have subscales, but you want to know the reliability of measuring a general factor (bifactor model) if you were to sum across all items and treat the entire scale as one scale, not multiple subscales. If hierarchical omega is high, it means your scale appears to reliably measure one construct even after accounting for subscales. I'm not 100% sure of this, to be frank, but that question is not particularly interesting to me, so I tend to stick with omega 2.

messages.subject: Re: negative variance with the "measurementInvariance" comand in lavaan - Where?
messages.subject_clean: negative variance with the "measurementInvariance" comand in lavaan - Where?
messages.body_plain:
> a) Is it normal to have the same significance from the Chi Square difference model for all 3 models [MeasurementInvariance]? What is this caused by? How can i fixed it?

No, that would indicate the models fit the same number of parameters.  Your measurementInvariace() output shows that the models all have increasing df and chi-squared values, as more constraints are added on measurement parameters.  So I'm not sure what you think needs fixing.

> b) Where is the reported negative variance? In my output I only see negative covariance for loyality~~experience. Is this the problematic part? How can I fix this?

No, covariances / correlations can be negative.  The model summary (fit3) you showed is a single-group model with regression paths between the latent factors.  So that is not any of the models fit in the measurementInvariance() function, which are multiple-group CFA models.

If you want to investigate the models fit by the measurementInvariance() function, you can save the output:

fits <- measurementInvariance(...)
fit.config <- fits[["fit.configural"]]
fit.metric <- fits[["fit.loadings"]]
fit.scalar <- fits[["fit.intercepts"]]

summary(fit.config) # no equality constraints across groups
summary(fit.metric) # constrained loadings
summary(fit.scalar) # constrained loadings and intercepts

> Is it normal to have the same significance, 3 times? What is this caused by? How can i fixed it?

These aren't times, they are groups.  But you need to consider them in sequence.  The configural model fits well, but there is significantly worse fit after constraining loadings.  Until you resolve why, there is no point considering any further constraints (it makes no sense to constrain an intercept for an item when the loading cannot be constrained).  If you are unfamiliar with the concepts, I recommend not doing any more analysis until you understand what you are doing.  Roger Millsap wrote a great comprehensive book on the topic:

https://books.google.com/books/about/Statistical_Approaches_to_Measurement_In.html?id=7HisAgAAQBAJ&hl=en

To investigate why loading-invariance failed, you would need to test each item's constraint.  The partial() function (also in the semTools package, like measurementInvariance())  could be useful.

> And the famous error message:

There are no error messages, only warnings.  The model converges, but it is warning you about a Heywood case, which may or may not indicate a problem.  Since you configural model fits well, the 95% CI for the negative variance might include positive values, indicating the Heywood case may mere by due to sampling variance.

summary(fit, ci = TRUE)

Terrence D. Jorgensen
Postdoctoral Researcher, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam
UvA web page: http://www.uva.nl/profile/t.d.jorgensen

messages.subject: Re: Composite reliability (CFA)
messages.body_plain:
The topic of this thread has drifted substantially but here are a few additional thoughts.

If the question is which estimates to report, there is a growing literature of simulation studies offering guidance.

If the question is how to report a given estimate, that was the question for which I suggested SEMNET.

There is probably some room for different perspectives.  I find omega3 attractive precisely because it will be more conservative.  If substantial difference emerge between the three omegas, that may indicate violations of the assumptions of omega1 and/or omega2.

The advantages gained from choosing one estimate over another may be relatively small in relation to the benefits of reporting an interval estimate instead of just a point estimate.  I am aware of three basic options:
1. Compute the reliability estimate as a defined parameter in the model syntax (you can check the point estimate against reliability() as a test of accuracy).
2. Use the boot package to bootstrap a standard error around the point estimate from reliability()
3. Use the ci.reliability() function from the MBESS package.  (A CI for alpha is also available from the rela package.)

Keith

------------------------
Keith A. Markus
John Jay College of Criminal Justice, CUNY
http://jjcweb.jjay.cuny.edu/kmarkus
Frontiers of Test Validity Theory: Measurement, Causation and Meaning.
http://www.routledge.com/books/details/9781841692203/

On 05/27/2017 08:11 AM, 'Anna' via lavaan wrote:
> My problem is that in the output RMSEA is 0.00 (which is actually good

All of this has one simple explanation: you have df=0, because you have
fitted a saturated model: there are as many free parameters as sample
statistics.

There is nothing wrong with this. But as your fit is already perfect,
fit indices are useless, and modification indices (suggesting how to
improve your fit) can not be computed.

Yves.

messages.subject: Poisson distributions and suppression effects
messages.body_plain:
Hi everyone,

I would like your advices/help on a model I’m working on. Imagine that I have a questionnaire and I’m trying to test relation among variables. I’m running a CFA model as follow:

 <https://lh3.googleusercontent.com/-MzuH-RP0pX8/WSnG_Kh2VXI/AAAAAAAAAhM/PwQi0wcuKy4-Jx2RAYRGe--GpJKan0jdQCLcB/s1600/schema.png>

Those variables are all observed somehow continuous (and if there were not, I recoded them in 7 categories according to Rhemtuall et al., 2012). Few problems emerged though:

1) If the main DV (or the mediators, which are also DVs for the left-part of the model) has a poisson distribution, is is still possible to run a CFA/SEM model under lavaan?

2) Let’s say I’m interested of the main effect of the IV on the DV but I also want to investigate 2 pathways (med1 and med2). Is there a way in lavaan to attest for how much of the relation between IV/DV is explained by the overall model?

3) If I run a univariate regression between the IV and the main DV, I found no significant effect. However, if I run the overall model above, I found a significant positive link between the IV and the DV along with negative link between IV-med1/2 and positive link between med1/2-DV. Does that mean there is a suppressive effect of the mediators? It seems difficult to interpret.

4) Finally, if I want to compare the results of this model across groups, I have been told that beyond 10 groups it’s difficult to run that in lavaan. But if I run it through let’s say 50 groups and found the same effects (the same magnitude), it actually strengthen my claim. Is that a technical limit to lavaan or more an interpretation problem?

Thanks in advance for all your help,

Jordane

messages.subject: Re: Poisson distributions and suppression effects
messages.body_plain:
> Those variables are all observed somehow continuous (and if there were not, I recoded them in 7 categories according to Rhemtuall et al., 2012).

If your variables are continuous, don't discretize them into 7 categories, just leave  them as they are.  Rhemtulla et al. were simply saying  if you have as little as 5-7 categories, that's almost as good as more ordered categories or approximate continuity.

> 1) If the main DV (or the mediators, which are also DVs for the left-part of the model) has a poisson distribution, is is still possible to run a CFA/SEM model under lavaan?

No, the Poisson link is not available in lavaan.

> 2) Let’s say I’m interested of the main effect of the IV on the DV but I also want to investigate 2 pathways (med1 and med2). Is there a way in lavaan to attest for how much of the relation between IV/DV is explained by the overall model?

If you want to see the change in R-squared, you can get it the same way you would in OLS regression.  Run the model with and without estimating the direct effect of IV on DV, and see how much R-squared changes.  You can print R-squared for endogenous variables in the summary() or parameterEstimates() output by setting the argument rsquare = TRUE.

> 3) If I run a univariate regression between the IV and the main DV, I found no significant effect. However, if I run the overall model above, I found a significant positive link between the IV and the DV along with negative link between IV-med1/2 and positive link between med1/2-DV. Does that mean there is a suppressive effect of the mediators? It seems difficult to interpret.

Here is an article you can read on the topic:

https://link.springer.com/article/10.1023/A:1026595011371

You can also ask non-lavaan questions like this on the general forum SEMNET:

www2.gsu.edu/~mkteer/semnet.html <http://www2.gsu.edu/~mkteer/semnet.html>

> 4) Finally, if I want to compare the results of this model across groups, I have been told that beyond 10 groups it’s difficult to run that in lavaan. But if I run it through let’s say 50 groups and found the same effects (the same magnitude), it actually strengthen my claim. Is that a technical limit to lavaan or more an interpretation problem?

If you have that many groups, I can't imagine you are interested in fixed effects of any particular group compared to another.  lavaan is capable of running a 2-level model in the development version:

install.packages("lavaan", repos="http://www.da.ugent.be", type="source")

If this is the approach you are interested in, Yves posted some instructional slides here:

http://users.ugent.be/~yrosseel/lavaan/jena2017/Jena_practical.pdf

Terrence D. Jorgensen
Postdoctoral Researcher, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam
UvA web page: http://www.uva.nl/profile/t.d.jorgensen

Yes, that's exactly it.  If those are the same variable, that implies their relationships with any other variable (e.g., with f1, with f2, etc.) would be identical. On Friday, 26 May 2017 17:12:49 UTC+2, Terrence Jorgensen wrote:
> > a) Is it normal to have the same significance from the Chi Square difference model for all 3 models [MeasurementInvariance]? What is this caused by? How can i fixed it?
>
> No, that would indicate the models fit the same number of parameters.  Your measurementInvariace() output shows that the models all have increasing df and chi-squared values, as more constraints are added on measurement parameters.  So I'm not sure what you think needs fixing.
>
> > b) Where is the reported negative variance? In my output I only see negative covariance for loyality~~experience. Is this the problematic part? How can I fix this?
>
> No, covariances / correlations can be negative.  The model summary (fit3) you showed is a single-group model with regression paths between the latent factors.  So that is not any of the models fit in the measurementInvariance() function, which are multiple-group CFA models.
>
> If you want to investigate the models fit by the measurementInvariance() function, you can save the output:
>
> fits <- measurementInvariance(...)
> fit.config <- fits[["fit.configural"]]
> fit.metric <- fits[["fit.loadings"]]
> fit.scalar <- fits[["fit.intercepts"]]
>
> summary(fit.config) # no equality constraints across groups
> summary(fit.metric) # constrained loadings
> summary(fit.scalar) # constrained loadings and intercepts
>
>
> > Is it normal to have the same significance, 3 times? What is this caused by? How can i fixed it?
>
> These aren't times, they are groups.  But you need to consider them in sequence.  The configural model fits well, but there is significantly worse fit after constraining loadings.  Until you resolve why, there is no point considering any further constraints (it makes no sense to constrain an intercept for an item when the loading cannot be constrained).  If you are unfamiliar with the concepts, I recommend not doing any more analysis until you understand what you are doing.  Roger Millsap wrote a great comprehensive book on the topic:
>
> https://books.google.com/books/about/Statistical_Approaches_to_Measurement_In.html?id=7HisAgAAQBAJ&hl=en
>
> To investigate why loading-invariance failed, you would need to test each item's constraint.  The partial() function (also in the semTools package, like measurementInvariance())  could be useful.
>
> > And the famous error message:
>
> There are no error messages, only warnings.  The model converges, but it is warning you about a Heywood case, which may or may not indicate a problem.  Since you configural model fits well, the 95% CI for the negative variance might include positive values, indicating the Heywood case may mere by due to sampling variance.
>
> summary(fit, ci = TRUE)
>
> Terrence D. Jorgensen
> Postdoctoral Researcher, Methods and Statistics
> Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam
> UvA web page: http://www.uva.nl/profile/t.d.jorgensen
>

>> a) Is it normal to have the same significance from the Chi Square
>>> difference model for all 3 models [MeasurementInvariance]? What is this
>>> caused by? How can i fixed it?

>>
>> No, that would indicate the models fit the same number of parameters.
>> Your
>> measurementInvariace() output shows that the models all have increasing

>> *df* and chi-squared values, as more constraints are added on measurement

>>
>> parameters.  So I'm not sure what you think needs fixing.
>>
>> b) Where is the reported negative variance? In my output I only see
>>> negative covariance for loyality~~experience. Is this the problematic
>>> part?
>>> How can I fix this?
>>>
>>
>> No, covariances / correlations can be negative.  The model summary (fit3)
>>
>> you showed is a single-group model with regression paths between the
>> latent
>> factors.  So that is not any of the models fit in the
>> measurementInvariance() function, which are multiple-group CFA models.
>>
>> If you want to investigate the models fit by the measurementInvariance()
>> function, you
>> can save the output:
>>
>> fits <- measurementInvariance(...)
>> fit.config <- fits[["fit.configural"]]
>> fit.metric <- fits[["fit.loadings"]]
>> fit.scalar <- fits[["fit.intercepts"]]
>>
>> summary(fit.config) # no equality constraints across groups
>> summary(fit.metric) # constrained loadings
>> summary(fit.scalar) # constrained loadings and intercepts
>>
>>
>>
>>> Is it normal to have the same significance, 3 times? What is this caused
>>>
>>> by? How can i fixed it?
>>>
>>
>> These aren't times, they are groups.  But you need to consider them in
>> sequence.  The configural model fits well, but there is significantly
>> worse
>> fit after constraining loadings.  Until you resolve why, there is no point
>>
>> considering any further constraints (it makes no sense to constrain an
>> intercept for an item when the loading cannot be constrained).  If you are
>>
>> unfamiliar with the concepts, I recommend not doing any more analysis
>> until
>> you understand what you are doing.  Roger Millsap wrote a great
>> comprehensive book on the topic:
>>
>>
>> https://books.google.com/books/about/Statistical_Approaches_to_Measurement_In.html?id=7HisAgAAQBAJ&hl=en
>>
>> To investigate why loading-invariance failed, you would need to test each
>>
>> item's constraint.  The partial() function (also in the semTools package,
>>
>> like measurementInvariance())  could be useful.
>>

>> And the famous *error message:*

>>>
>>
>> There are no error messages, only warnings.  The model converges, but it
>> is warning you about a Heywood case, which may or may not indicate a
>> problem.  Since you configural model fits well, the 95% CI for the
>> negative
>> variance might include positive values, indicating the Heywood case may
>> mere by due to sampling variance.
>>
>> summary(fit, ci = TRUE)

messages.subject: Growth cuve analysis: time (in)variant predictors
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

I am trying to replicate a paper from Hox & Stoel 2005, in which they tested a growth curve model with time variant and invariant predictors.
I get quite a different Chi2 (almost twice as large) and RMSEA. Also, I noticed when plotting my model, that the growth() function automaticaly adds covariances
between the invariant predictor (z) and the time-variant predictors (x0-3).Also, covariances between x0-3 are added automatically whilst these are not latent variables.
I thought this was quite strange and tried to remove this by setting: auto.cov.y = FALSE,
but this doesn't change anything (I think true is the default in growth() and this cannot be changed?).

Anyone knows where these covariances come from?

My model code is quite standard:

#Model 3 with time variant and invariant regressors
GCMmodel3 <- '
#Slope and Intercept
B0 =~ 1*Y0 + 1*Y1 + 1*Y2 + 1*Y3
B1 =~ 0*Y0 + 1*Y1 + 2*Y2 + 3*Y3

# #Equal variances of error (homoskedasticity)
Y0~~ label("Ve")*Y0
Y1~~ equal("Ve")*Y1
Y2~~ equal("Ve")*Y2
Y3~~ equal("Ve")*Y3

# time-varying covariates (equalized as in Stoel et al., 2004)
Y0 ~ TVC*X0
Y1 ~ TVC*X1
Y2 ~ TVC*X2
Y3 ~ TVC*X3

# time-invariant covariate
B0 ~ Z
B1 ~ Z
'
Hopefully, anyone knows why these covariances (mmainly between z and x0-4) keep popping up!
Many thanks!!
Carolien

On Tuesday, May 23, 2017 at 9:45:36 PM UTC+2, Terrence Jorgensen wrote:
> >
> > 1. How do i measure the (significant) differences between group 1 and group 2 regarding mediation output? (i thought of something with the anova function, but not sure how).
>
> I'm not sure I understand your question.  There is a significance test reported to the right of the estimates.  If you want to test whether the indirect path (or a and/or b paths) differ significantly between groups, then yes, you can fit another model where you assign different labels for each group (so they are not constrained to equality, like they are in your model), then use anova() to compare the fit of the models to test the null hypothesis that the more constrained model fits just as well as the less constrained model.
>
> > 2. The 'defined' parameters output, does this regard the total model?
>
> It regards the parameters you defined.  Because you assigned the same labels (a and b) for both groups, they are constrained to equality across groups.
>
> http://lavaan.ugent.be/tutorial/groups.html
>
> If you give those parameters different labels in each group, you will have to define the indirect and total effects separately for each group, and both will show up in the output.
>
> Terrence D. Jorgensen
> Postdoctoral Researcher, Methods and Statistics
> Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam
